arguments.name: Cosmological argument
arguments.summary: The existence, dependence, or beginning of the universe is used to argue for an ultimate cause or explanation.
arguments.body: Cosmological arguments are a family rather than one proof. A contingency version begins with things that could have failed to exist and asks for an explanation of their existence; a causal version reasons from causes or a beginning. Some versions conclude only that there is a necessary ground or first cause. Further argument is needed to identify that ground with a personal God and attribute divine properties. The premise sets below represent a contingency-style reconstruction.
arguments.origin: Aquinas's Five Ways (13th century), with earlier and later variants; this reconstruction follows a contingency form discussed in natural theology.
premises: At least one contingent thing exists.
The existence of contingent things calls for an explanation beyond simply restating that they exist.
An explanatory chain consisting only of contingent things does not fully explain why any contingent things exist.
arguments.conclusion: There is some necessary ground or explanation of contingent reality.
assumptions: A sufficiently strong principle of explanation is true for contingent existence.
The explanatory regress cannot be left as an unexplained totality.
The conclusion does not alone establish that the necessary ground is the God of any particular religion.

objections.objection: The universe or totality of contingent things may simply be a brute fact.
objections.reply: A defender can argue that brute contingency is less satisfying than a necessary ground, but must explain why explanatory demand applies to the totality.

objections.objection: An infinite regress of contingent causes may be possible.
objections.reply: The contingency defender can say that an infinite chain still leaves unexplained why the chain exists at all; critics dispute whether the whole needs a further cause.

objections.objection: Even a necessary ground need not be personal or unique.
objections.reply: This objection limits what follows. The defender must offer separate arguments for further divine attributes.

examples.text: Every book in a library has an author, but the library as a whole may not have a further author.
examples.note: The analogy questions whether explanations of members automatically explain a whole; cosmological defenders distinguish an aggregate from the existence of the entire contingent series.

arguments.name: Dream and skeptical argument
arguments.summary: Because dreams can feel like waking experience, present experience alone may not prove that one is awake.
arguments.body: Descartes observes that he has sometimes dreamed experiences much like waking ones. If there is no infallible mark distinguishing waking from dreaming, sensory experience may fail to establish that the external world is as it appears. The argument motivates suspension about particular perceptual beliefs, not necessarily the conclusion that we are dreaming. Descartes later tries to recover knowledge through further premises about God and clear perception, which are themselves disputed.
arguments.origin: René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy (1641), Meditation I.
premises: Dreams can present experiences that seem vivid and coherent while they occur.
The current experience could be a dream indistinguishable from waking experience by the features considered so far.
If two incompatible scenarios fit all available evidence, that evidence alone does not establish which scenario obtains.
arguments.conclusion: Current sensory experience alone may not provide certainty that one is awake or that the external world is as perceived.
assumptions: The goal is certainty or knowledge that excludes skeptical alternatives.
A dream possibility is epistemically relevant even if it is not probable.
Evidence from memory and coherence may not decisively distinguish waking from dreaming.

objections.objection: Waking life has stable continuity and shared verification absent in ordinary dreams.
objections.reply: A skeptic can ask whether these are known directly or inferred from within experience; a fallibilist replies that they still provide strong, defeasible evidence.

objections.objection: The possibility of error does not erase knowledge.
objections.reply: The argument targets infallibilist standards; externalists and contextualists can deny that knowledge requires ruling out every skeptical scenario.

objections.objection: Dreaming is not genuinely indistinguishable once examined carefully.
objections.reply: Descartes uses the possibility to motivate doubt, not to claim all dreams are perfect replicas; critics can narrow the scenario's reach.

examples.text: A dreamer seems to be sitting by a fire, then wakes and finds no fire.
examples.note: The remembered resemblance illustrates why the experience's felt vividness may not settle whether it is waking.

arguments.name: Experience machine argument
arguments.summary: If a life of simulated pleasure seems worse than a real life, pleasure alone may not make a life go well.
arguments.body: Nozick asks whether people would choose a machine that guarantees the experiences they most want while concealing that they are simulated. Many judge that they would lose something important: doing things rather than merely seeming to do them, being a certain kind of person, or living in contact with reality. The argument challenges hedonism about well-being; it does not by itself prove that pleasure has no value or settle every theory of welfare.
arguments.origin: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), chapter 3.
premises: A machine can provide a life of experiences as pleasant and varied as the experiences a person would choose.
Many people would refuse permanent connection, even with assurance the experiences would be indistinguishable from real life.
Their refusal is best explained by valuing something beyond pleasant experience.
arguments.conclusion: Pleasure or experience alone does not exhaust what makes a life go well.
assumptions: Intuitions about the hypothetical are reliable enough to bear on theories of well-being.
The refusal is motivated by a good such as reality or agency, rather than fear, distrust, or status quo bias.

objections.objection: People may refuse because they distrust the machine, not because reality has independent value.
objections.reply: The thought experiment stipulates reliable operation and asks whether refusal persists under trust; critics can still reject the stipulation's psychological plausibility.

objections.objection: The case shows only that people value contact with reality, not that contact makes their lives better.
objections.reply: A defender can distinguish wanting something from its contribution to welfare, but argues that ordinary welfare judgments treat genuine achievement and relationships as goods.

objections.objection: The choice is too extreme to test everyday hedonism.
objections.reply: The case is designed to isolate whether experience is the only intrinsic good; it needs support from other examples to establish a general theory.

examples.text: A person can have simulated friendships that feel perfect but chooses to remain with real friends despite ordinary conflict.
examples.note: This tests whether genuine relationships matter independently of the pleasant feelings they generate.

arguments.name: Fine-tuning argument
arguments.summary: Life-permitting physical parameters are taken to support an explanation, sometimes a designer, over chance alone.
arguments.body: The argument starts from the claim that some basic physical parameters fall within a narrow range compatible with complex life. It then compares hypotheses: design, chance, deeper physical necessity, or a multiverse with selection effects. The observation can favor design only if the relevant probability distributions and the designer's likely aims are specified. Existing observers necessarily find themselves in observer-compatible conditions, so selection effects matter. This is a probabilistic argument and its scientific and philosophical premises remain contested.
arguments.origin: Contemporary philosophy of religion and cosmology; major formulations include Robin Collins's fine-tuning argument.
premises: Some parameters in current physical models appear to lie in ranges that permit complex life.
A life-permitting range is not otherwise physically necessary, and its probability under a chance model is low.
The observed life-permitting conditions are more expected under a suitably specified design hypothesis than under relevant alternatives.
arguments.conclusion: The fine-tuning data provide some evidence for design, if the probability comparison is well grounded.
assumptions: The parameter range and probability measure are meaningful and scientifically defensible.
Observer selection is accounted for rather than mistaken for independent evidence.
The design hypothesis predicts life-permitting conditions better than deeper-law or multiverse accounts.

objections.objection: There is no well-established probability distribution over possible constants.
objections.reply: A defender can argue that some comparisons remain informative without exact probabilities, but the evidential strength is then less precise.

objections.objection: Observers can only observe conditions compatible with observers, creating a selection effect.
objections.reply: A defender can compare observer-conditioned predictions across hypotheses; the critic argues this may remove much of the apparent surprise.

objections.objection: A multiverse or unknown physical law could explain the observed values.
objections.reply: A defender can note that these alternatives also require support and may shift rather than eliminate explanatory questions.

examples.text: A person draws a life-permitting universe from a hypothetical vast set of parameter combinations.
examples.note: The example frames why a narrow life-permitting range might look surprising, while the draw's probability model is itself disputed.

arguments.name: Is–ought argument
arguments.summary: A normative conclusion does not follow from purely descriptive premises without some normative bridge premise.
arguments.body: Hume observes that writers sometimes move from statements about what is to claims about what ought to be without explaining the transition. A careful reconstruction is a logical point: descriptive premises alone do not entail a normative conclusion unless a normative rule or bridge principle is supplied. This does not show that facts are irrelevant to ethics, nor that no normative truths can be known. It asks that the inferential work connecting facts to obligations be made explicit.
arguments.origin: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), Book III, Part I, Section I.
premises: A valid deductive argument's conclusion must be entailed by its premises.
Purely descriptive premises can all be true while a normative conclusion is false.
Therefore, a normative conclusion is not deductively entailed by descriptive premises alone.
arguments.conclusion: Any deduction from facts to an obligation requires at least one normative bridge premise.
assumptions: The distinction between descriptive and normative statements is clear enough for the argument at hand.
The target inference claims entailment, rather than a defeasible or explanatory relation.
The conclusion concerns logical support and does not rule out deriving values from a broader theory with normative premises.

objections.objection: Some facts appear inherently normative, so the descriptive/normative split may be false.
objections.reply: A defender can ask whether the supposedly descriptive fact already contains normative content; that would make the bridge explicit rather than eliminate the issue.

objections.objection: Moral conclusions can be supported inductively by facts.
objections.reply: The argument concerns entailment from purely descriptive premises; inductive support can still depend on background normative commitments.

objections.objection: Hume's passage may concern motivation rather than a formal logical gap.
objections.reply: The standard is–ought reading is influential but debated; the reconstruction should not be treated as the only interpretation of Hume.

examples.text: All actions that maximize happiness are common; therefore, everyone ought to maximize happiness.
examples.note: The conclusion needs a normative principle connecting commonness or happiness with obligation.

arguments.name: Mary's room knowledge argument
arguments.summary: If Mary learns every physical fact about color vision while seeing only black and white, seeing red may teach her something new.
arguments.body: Frank Jackson asks us to imagine Mary, an excellent scientist who knows all physical facts about color vision but has lived in a monochrome environment. On first seeing red, she seems to learn what red looks like. If she already possessed all physical knowledge, the new knowledge appears to be nonphysical knowledge, challenging physicalism. The thought experiment's force depends on what kind of knowledge she gains and whether that knowledge is a new fact or a new ability or mode of acquaintance.
arguments.origin: Frank Jackson, “Epiphenomenal Qualia” (1982) and “What Mary Didn't Know” (1986).
premises: Before leaving her room, Mary knows all the physical facts about human color vision.
After seeing red, Mary learns something she did not know before.
If Mary gains knowledge, what she learns is a fact rather than only an ability or acquaintance.
arguments.conclusion: There are facts about conscious experience that are not physical facts, so physicalism is incomplete.
assumptions: A complete physical description is compatible with Mary's not having first-person color experience.
The epistemic gap indicates an ontological gap only if the new knowledge is genuinely propositional knowledge of a fact.

objections.objection: Mary gains an ability to recognize or imagine red, not new factual knowledge.
objections.reply: Jackson's defender can ask whether Mary could truly say nothing factual that she learns; the dispute turns on whether abilities exhaust the change.

objections.objection: She gains acquaintance with a familiar physical fact under a new mode of presentation.
objections.reply: A defender can argue that knowing a fact by acquaintance is still knowledge, while the physicalist replies that this does not establish a new nonphysical fact.

objections.objection: The setup's claim that Mary knows all physical facts may be incoherent if experience is needed to grasp them.
objections.reply: The thought experiment stipulates extensive theoretical knowledge to isolate whether description alone captures experience; the stipulation itself remains open to challenge.

examples.text: Mary reads every scientific account of color vision but has never seen red; then she sees a red tomato.
examples.note: The alleged change motivates the argument, while whether it is new knowledge or a new capacity is the central dispute.

arguments.name: Ontological argument
aliases: Argument from the concept of God
arguments.summary: Anselm reasons from the concept of God as unsurpassably great toward God's necessary existence.
arguments.body: Unlike arguments from observed causes or design, ontological arguments begin with a concept or possibility claim. Anselm's Proslogion argument says that God is that than which no greater can be conceived, and that existing in reality is greater than existing only in understanding. Later modal versions argue that if a necessarily existing God is possible, then God exists necessarily. These are distinct formulations; the premises here sketch Anselm's original strategy, whose move from a concept to existence is disputed.
arguments.origin: Anselm of Canterbury, Proslogion (1077–78); later modal versions are not identical to Anselm's text.
premises: God is understood as that than which no greater can be conceived.
A being that exists in reality is greater than an otherwise matching being that exists only in the understanding.
If God existed only in the understanding, a greater being could be conceived: one existing in reality.
arguments.conclusion: God exists in reality.
assumptions: Existence can function as a greatness-making feature in the relevant comparison.
The concept is coherent and refers to a possible being.
A definition or concept can support an existential conclusion only with substantive premises beyond the definition itself.

objections.objection: Existence is not a property that makes an object greater, as Kant argues.
objections.reply: Anselm's defender may say the argument concerns unsurpassable greatness or necessary existence, not ordinary existence as a quality; critics question whether that avoids the objection.

objections.objection: The reasoning would seem to prove a perfect island or another maximally great object.
objections.reply: A defender can reply that necessary existence may apply coherently only to a unique ultimate being; the burden is to show why the parody differs.

objections.objection: The concept of a maximally great being may be incoherent.
objections.reply: A defender must establish coherence independently; the argument cannot treat the possibility premise as cost-free.

examples.text: Someone defines a perfect island as the greatest island conceivable and claims it must exist.
examples.note: The parody pressures the inference from a description to reality; a defender distinguishes contingent islands from a necessarily existing being.

arguments.name: Open question argument
arguments.summary: If it remains meaningful to ask whether something good is good, goodness may not be identical to a natural property used to define it.
arguments.body: Moore argues that for any proposed naturalistic definition of good, such as pleasant, it remains an intelligible question whether what is pleasant is good. If the terms named the same property, the question would be like asking whether a bachelor is unmarried: answerable by meaning alone. Moore takes this to show that goodness is simple and indefinable, not that no natural property can correlate with goodness. Later philosophers dispute whether the argument defeats identity claims, especially when identities are informative or a posteriori.
arguments.origin: G. E. Moore, Principia Ethica (1903), §§10–14.
premises: If good were identical by definition with a natural property such as pleasure, asking whether pleasure is good would be closed by meaning.
The question whether pleasure is good remains intelligible and apparently unresolved by definition.
A meaningful open question indicates that the proposed definition does not capture the meaning of good.
arguments.conclusion: Good cannot be defined as identical to any proposed natural property in the way considered.
assumptions: Meaningful questions reveal facts about the meanings of their terms.
The target definition is meant as an analysis of meaning, not merely a claim about property identity.
A posteriori identities can be questioned as open without thereby being false, a challenge to Moore's inference.

objections.objection: An identity can be true yet informative, as with water and H2O, so a question can remain open despite identity.
objections.reply: Moore's defender can distinguish conceptual definitions from empirical identities; critics argue that this leaves many naturalist analyses untouched.

objections.objection: The question may be open because the speaker lacks information, not because meanings differ.
objections.reply: A defender can say Moore's test concerns what is settled by understanding the words alone, but the test remains sensitive to context and competence.

objections.objection: The argument shows at most that 'good' is not synonymous with a natural term.
objections.reply: Moore's own conclusion is modestly semantic in that respect; further argument is needed to establish metaphysical non-naturalism.

examples.text: Someone asks whether every pleasant act is morally good even after understanding the word 'pleasant'.
examples.note: The question seems substantive rather than settled by the meanings of the words, which is the test Moore emphasizes.

arguments.name: Pascal’s wager
arguments.summary: Under uncertainty about God, Pascal argues that the practical stakes can rationally favor wagering for belief.
arguments.body: Pascal frames belief as a practical choice under uncertainty. If God exists, the gain associated with belief may be infinite; if God does not, the loss may be finite. On some decision-theoretic assumptions, even a small positive probability of God can make the expected value of belief outweigh its costs. Pascal also discusses cultivating belief through practice. The wager is not a proof that God exists, and its outcome table, probability assumptions, and treatment of competing religions are disputed.
arguments.origin: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, fragment commonly numbered 233; several related wagers appear in the passage.
premises: A person must choose how to live despite uncertainty about God.
If God exists, the relevant religious outcome may have infinite or extremely high value.
If God does not exist, the cost of wagering for belief is finite.
A positive probability of the favorable outcome can dominate expected utility calculations.
arguments.conclusion: Under the wager’s assumptions, a person has practical reason to wager for belief or to cultivate it.
assumptions: The possible outcomes and utilities are represented adequately by the wager.
A nonzero probability can be assigned to the relevant conception of God.
Belief or belief-cultivation is sufficiently under voluntary control.

objections.objection: Different religions offer incompatible wagers, and the table may omit them.
objections.reply: A defender can try to compare a broader set of possibilities, but that increases the difficulty of assigning probabilities and utilities.

objections.objection: Belief is not directly chosen, and acting as if one believes may not produce genuine belief.
objections.reply: Pascal’s practical proposal includes habits and participation that might shape belief indirectly; whether that is epistemically appropriate remains disputed.

objections.objection: Infinite utility can make expected-value calculations unstable or yield implausible conclusions.
objections.reply: Defenders can use finite or nonstandard decision models, though these change the force and details of the wager.

examples.text: A traveler uncertain whether a bridge is safe may choose the cautious route when the cost is small and the possible loss is severe.
examples.note: The analogy illustrates practical choice under asymmetric stakes; religious belief adds distinct questions about probability, agency, and competing outcomes.

arguments.name: Philosophical zombie argument
arguments.summary: If a physical duplicate without conscious experience is genuinely possible, physical facts may not fully determine consciousness.
arguments.body: A philosophical zombie is stipulated to be physically and behaviorally like a conscious person but to lack phenomenal experience. The argument moves from the apparent conceivability of such a being to its metaphysical possibility, then from possibility to a challenge to physicalism. It is a modal argument, not an empirical claim that zombies exist. The crucial transition from conceivability to possibility is disputed, and some physicalists argue our concepts make the scenario seem coherent when it is not.
arguments.origin: Modern conceivability arguments associated with David Chalmers; related debates include Joseph Levine's explanatory gap.
premises: A physical duplicate of a conscious person without phenomenal experience is coherently conceivable.
If such a scenario is ideally conceivable, it is metaphysically possible.
If physicalism is true, a physical duplicate cannot differ in phenomenal consciousness.
arguments.conclusion: Physicalism is false or incomplete about phenomenal consciousness.
assumptions: Conceivability tracks metaphysical possibility in this case.
Phenomenal consciousness is not identical to or fixed by physical facts.
The description of a zombie is internally coherent rather than merely verbally describable.

objections.objection: Conceivability is fallible and does not establish possibility.
objections.reply: A defender can argue that the conceivability is ideal and persists after reflection; the physicalist replies that apparent conceivability can reflect incomplete concepts.

objections.objection: A posteriori identities can be necessary despite seeming separable, as water and H2O.
objections.reply: The zombie defender argues that consciousness differs because the phenomenal concept appears to reveal experience directly; critics dispute that special status.

objections.objection: The argument assumes a controversial view of phenomenal consciousness.
objections.reply: It is intended to expose that commitment, not to settle it without further argument.

examples.text: Imagine a molecule-for-molecule duplicate of a person who behaves normally but has no felt experience.
examples.note: If this description is genuinely possible, it challenges the claim that physical duplication guarantees experience.

arguments.name: Private language argument
arguments.summary: A language whose signs are meaningful only through one person's inaccessible private impressions may lack standards for correct use.
arguments.body: Wittgenstein's discussion in Philosophical Investigations §§243–315 is complex and not universally agreed to be one compact proof. A common reconstruction considers a person who privately names a sensation and records each recurrence. If the only test of correct application is that it seems right to the person, there is no independent distinction between seeming correct and being correct. The target is a language in principle inaccessible to any possible community, not the ordinary privacy of sensations or private note-taking.
arguments.origin: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (1953), §§243–315; the label is a later scholarly grouping.
premises: A sign has meaning only if there is a distinction between using it correctly and merely seeming to use it correctly.
In the proposed private language, only the speaker's present impression can determine whether a sign is used correctly.
A memory impression cannot independently certify that the present use matches the original rule.
arguments.conclusion: A language whose meanings are in principle private to one speaker cannot establish stable rules of meaning in the proposed way.
assumptions: Meaningful rule-following requires criteria beyond an uncheckable impression of correctness.
A solitary speaker cannot establish such criteria through memory alone.
The argument concerns a language in principle private, not a language that others happen not to understand.

objections.objection: A speaker can privately define a sign by attending carefully to a sensation.
objections.reply: A defender can ask what distinguishes correct re-identification from the speaker's feeling of correctness; the critic may assume public criteria too quickly.

objections.objection: A private diary can use meaningful terms without others checking every entry.
objections.reply: The argument need not deny private application; it challenges whether the criteria for the terms could be private in principle.

objections.objection: Wittgenstein's remarks may be a therapeutic discussion rather than a single deductive argument.
objections.reply: A defender can present the reconstruction as one strand in a broader critique of meaning, while acknowledging that scholars dispute its structure and conclusion.

examples.text: A person marks a private sensation with 'S' and later believes the same sensation has returned.
examples.note: Without an independent criterion, the person may only have the impression that the rule was followed.

arguments.name: Problem of evil argument
arguments.summary: Suffering in the world is offered as evidence against an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good God.
arguments.body: The familiar evidential form starts from severe suffering that appears to serve no greater good or prevent no comparable evil. It infers that such suffering is less expected if a perfectly good and powerful God exists than if no such God exists. This is an inductive challenge, not the simple deductive claim that any evil logically rules out God. Different versions use animal suffering, apparently pointless suffering, or the amount and distribution of harms; they need not share one exact premise set.
arguments.origin: Modern evidential formulation associated especially with William Rowe; earlier discussions include Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779).
premises: There is severe suffering in the world, including suffering that appears preventable without sacrificing a greater good.
A perfectly good and powerful being would prevent suffering unless it were necessary for a sufficient good or to prevent a greater evil.
At least some apparently pointless suffering is not necessary for such a good, as far as the available evidence indicates.
arguments.conclusion: The observed suffering lowers the probability that an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God exists.
assumptions: The key inference is probabilistic, not deductively valid from suffering alone.
Our inability to identify a justifying reason is evidence only if we have some ability to recognize such reasons.

objections.objection: Humans may be too limited to know the goods that justify suffering.
objections.reply: A defender can argue that finite perspective makes absence of a known reason weak evidence; the critic can ask whether this skepticism is applied consistently to other moral judgments.

objections.objection: Free will or stable natural laws may require the possibility of serious harm.
objections.reply: A defender can cite these goods, while the argument can focus on suffering not plausibly caused by free choices or necessary regularities, such as animal pain before humans.

objections.objection: A world with suffering may still be better overall than any feasible alternative.
objections.reply: That possibility blocks a deductive refutation; the evidential proponent replies that the scale and distribution still call for comparative support.

examples.text: A fawn dies slowly after a forest fire with no apparent human witness or benefit.
examples.note: Rowe uses cases of this kind to illustrate suffering that appears gratuitous; whether it truly is gratuitous is contested.

arguments.name: Problem of induction argument
arguments.summary: Past regularities do not logically guarantee that unobserved cases or the future will resemble them.
arguments.body: Hume's challenge asks what justifies projecting observed patterns beyond the observations. Deductive reasoning cannot establish that nature will remain uniform without assuming the very regularity at issue. A non-deductive defense seems to rely on past success, which is itself an inductive inference. The result is a problem about rational justification, not a demonstration that induction never works. Philosophers offer pragmatic, reliabilist, Bayesian, and naturalistic responses.
arguments.origin: David Hume, An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding (1748), section IV.
premises: Our beliefs about unobserved cases depend substantially on projecting patterns observed in past cases.
The future or unobserved need not logically resemble the past or observed.
A deductive justification would require a premise that nature is uniform.
An inductive justification of uniformity would already use the inference it is meant to justify.
arguments.conclusion: Induction lacks a non-circular deductive justification from experience alone.
assumptions: A justification must be deductive or independently non-circular to answer Hume's challenge.
Practical success or reliable cognitive methods may not count as the sought foundational justification.

objections.objection: The challenge demands an impossible kind of justification; induction can be rational without proof.
objections.reply: A defender of the problem can concede that practical rationality may not require proof while preserving the distinction between explanation of use and ultimate justification.

objections.objection: Induction is justified by its track record.
objections.reply: Hume's reply is that using past success to infer future success is precisely an inductive move, though reliabilists may accept that circularity as benign.

objections.objection: Bayesian updating can justify learning from evidence.
objections.reply: Bayesian methods formalize how evidence changes credence but do not alone show why the chosen priors or likelihoods are appropriate.

examples.text: The sun has risen every day observed, so someone expects it to rise tomorrow.
examples.note: The expectation is reasonable in ordinary practice, but the observed pattern does not entail the future outcome.

arguments.name: Problem of other minds argument
aliases: Argument from analogy to other minds
arguments.summary: We cannot directly experience another person's consciousness, so the problem asks how we are justified in believing they have it.
arguments.body: The traditional problem begins from an asymmetry: one's own experience is directly present, while another person's experience is inferred from behavior and bodily similarity. An analogical argument says that others behave as we do in circumstances where we feel pain, so they probably feel pain too. This is not a proof, and modern responses include inference to the best explanation, common-cause accounts, and embodied interaction. The challenge concerns justification, not whether other people actually have minds.
arguments.origin: A longstanding problem in modern philosophy; analogical formulations are associated with discussions by John Stuart Mill and others.
premises: I directly experience my own mental states but do not directly experience another person's.
Other people have bodies and behavior relevantly similar to mine.
In my case, certain bodily states and behaviors accompany mental states.
Relevant similarity gives some reason to infer similar mental states in others.
arguments.conclusion: Belief in other minds is inferential and requires an account of how that inference is justified.
assumptions: Behavior and bodily similarity provide evidence of experience rather than mere outward resemblance.
The argument from one's own case generalizes beyond one individual.
Direct access is not required for justified belief.

objections.objection: Analogy from one case is too weak to justify beliefs about many other minds.
objections.reply: A defender can supplement analogy with shared biology, behavior, and explanatory success; critics may challenge how those sources establish phenomenal experience.

objections.objection: Other minds are the best explanation of complex, flexible behavior.
objections.reply: An inference to the best explanation can answer the problem without claiming certainty; the skeptic can ask whether experience is needed to explain behavior.

objections.objection: The argument risks treating one's own case as the model for all minds.
objections.reply: A defender can limit the inference to sufficiently similar beings and use broader evidence for beings with different bodies or behavior.

examples.text: A friend winces, protects an injured hand, and reports pain.
examples.note: The combination of behavior, shared physiology, and testimony supports belief in pain without direct access to the friend's experience.

arguments.name: Singer's drowning child argument
arguments.summary: If you can prevent a serious harm at modest cost, distance alone does not usually remove your moral reason to help.
arguments.body: Singer's case asks whether a passerby should rescue a child drowning in a shallow pond, even if doing so ruins their clothes. Since the cost is small and the harm grave, the answer seems clear. Singer argues that the same principle applies to preventable suffering far away when aid is effective and does not require sacrificing something comparably important. The conclusion supports substantial aid, though the scope and demandingness of the principle remain disputed.
arguments.origin: Peter Singer, “Famine, Affluence, and Morality” (1972).
premises: If we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do so.
Donating a modest amount can effectively prevent serious suffering.
The fact that those in need are distant does not by itself make their claims less important.
arguments.conclusion: We have a moral obligation to give effective aid when its cost is not comparably serious.
assumptions: Comparable importance is an adequate standard for what sacrifices are permissible.
Distance and special relationships do not create a morally relevant difference in the cases under consideration.

objections.objection: The principle demands too much by requiring continued giving until further aid would be comparably costly.
objections.reply: Singer can accept that this is demanding and argue that comfort and luxury are not strong enough reasons to withhold life-saving aid.

objections.objection: Duties to nearby people or institutions may differ from duties to strangers.
objections.reply: The response is that special duties can matter without erasing a general duty to prevent grave harm when the cost is modest.

objections.objection: Donations may be ineffective or diverted.
objections.reply: The principle concerns effective prevention; uncertainty makes careful choice of aid important rather than eliminating the duty.

examples.text: You pass a shallow pond and can rescue a child at the cost of muddy clothes.
examples.note: The case makes the low cost and urgent harm salient before comparing it with distant aid.

arguments.name: Social contract argument
arguments.summary: Political authority or moral rules are justified by principles people would agree to under specified conditions.
arguments.body: Social contract arguments explain or justify rules by reference to agreement among people, often in a hypothetical state of nature or a fair choice situation. Hobbes emphasizes security under vulnerability; Rousseau asks how political association can preserve freedom; Rawls uses a hypothetical original position. These are not one doctrine. The reconstruction here captures a general justificatory pattern and makes clear that hypothetical consent is not the same as actual historical consent.
arguments.origin: A family of arguments in Hobbes, Rousseau, and Rawls; the premises below state a general pattern, not any one author's full theory.
premises: People have interests that can conflict and require common rules for coordination or protection.
Rules that could be accepted by persons under fair or appropriately specified conditions have a claim to legitimacy.
A proposed political arrangement provides terms that those persons could rationally accept.
arguments.conclusion: The arrangement has a contract-based justification or claim to legitimacy.
assumptions: The agreement conditions are fair and do not covertly dictate the answer.
Hypothetical agreement can carry justificatory force without actual consent.
The theory identifies whose agreement matters and what counts as rational acceptance.

objections.objection: No actual contract was signed, so citizens did not consent.
objections.reply: A defender replies that hypothetical agreement is a test of justifiability, not a historical event; critics question whether that is enough for political obligation.

objections.objection: People excluded from the imagined agreement may be dominated by its rules.
objections.reply: The defender must show that the conditions represent all affected persons fairly; exclusions can undermine the argument.

objections.objection: Different assumptions about human nature yield very different contracts.
objections.reply: That plurality shows the conclusion depends on the setup; proponents should defend those assumptions rather than present contract as a unique derivation.

examples.text: People accept a common authority because without shared rules each faces insecurity from others.
examples.note: This resembles Hobbes's rationale; it supports a particular contract argument, not every social contract theory.

arguments.name: Teleological argument
arguments.summary: Order or apparent purposiveness in nature is treated as evidence for an intelligent designer.
arguments.body: Design arguments infer purpose or intelligence from features of the world that resemble products of intelligence. Paley's watch analogy is a familiar version; Hume's Dialogues examines its limits. Modern forms may appeal to biological complexity or cosmic conditions. The inference is usually analogical or abductive, not a deduction from order alone. A designer hypothesis must be specified well enough to show why the observed order is more expected under it than under alternatives.
arguments.origin: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802); earlier discussion by David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779).
premises: Some features of nature display complex, coordinated order suited to particular functions.
In familiar cases, comparable functional order is produced by intelligence.
An intelligent cause makes the observed natural order more likely than relevant non-intelligent alternatives.
arguments.conclusion: An intelligent designer is a plausible explanation of some natural order.
assumptions: The analogy between natural structures and artifacts is sufficiently strong.
The designer hypothesis has independently motivated expectations about what would be designed.
An inference to a designer does not alone establish a perfect, unique, or religiously specific God.

objections.objection: Natural selection explains biological adaptation without foresight.
objections.reply: A defender can shift to features not explained by selection, such as initial conditions, but must not treat gaps in current knowledge as evidence by themselves.

objections.objection: The world contains waste, suffering, and disorder unlike what a perfect designer might be expected to make.
objections.reply: A defender can question whether human standards identify the designer's aims; that reply weakens the inference unless those aims are specified.

objections.objection: The analogy assumes a designer because artifacts and organisms look alike only superficially.
objections.reply: A defender can present the argument as comparative explanation rather than strict analogy, while the critic demands evidence that design predicts the data better.

examples.text: A watch found on a beach has interlocking parts arranged to keep time.
examples.note: Paley uses this kind of case to motivate design inference; Hume challenges how far the comparison extends to the universe.

arguments.name: Third Man argument
arguments.summary: Plato's dialogue Parmenides presses whether a Form of largeness requires another Form to explain what all large things share.
arguments.body: The Third Man is an internal challenge to a version of Plato's Forms theory, presented by Parmenides in Plato's dialogue. If many large things are large by sharing a separate Form of Largeness, and the Form itself is also large, then the original things and the Form appear to require a further Form explaining their common largeness. Repeating the explanation generates a regress. The dialogue explores multiple difficulties and does not simply report Plato's settled view; scholars dispute which formulation the objection targets.
arguments.origin: Plato, Parmenides, around 130e–132a; the label “Third Man” is traditional scholarly shorthand.
premises: Many particular things are large because they participate in a Form of Largeness.
The Form of Largeness is itself large, or the same explanatory predicate applies to it.
Whenever several things are F, a distinct Form is needed to explain their common F-ness.
arguments.conclusion: This version of the Forms theory generates an explanatory regress and requires revision or rejection.
assumptions: The relevant Form is itself a member of the class it explains.
The one-over-many principle applies without restriction to Forms and particulars alike.
A regress of Forms is vicious or fails to explain participation.

objections.objection: The Form need not be large in the same sense as particular large things.
objections.reply: A Platonist can distinguish predication of the Form from participation by particulars; the critic asks whether that distinction is independently justified.

objections.objection: The one-over-many principle can be restricted so it does not apply to the Form itself.
objections.reply: A defender of the objection says the restriction needs motivation and may weaken the explanatory account of shared properties.

objections.objection: Plato may be examining, rather than endorsing, the challenged theory.
objections.reply: The argument remains useful as a diagnostic objection even if the dialogue does not present a final doctrine.

examples.text: Several objects and the Form itself are all called large, prompting a further common Form.
examples.note: The example displays how an explanatory principle can appear to apply again to its own explanation.

arguments.name: Transcendental argument
arguments.summary: A transcendental argument infers necessary conditions for an experience or practice that is already accepted as real.
arguments.body: Rather than infer an unseen cause from an observed effect, a transcendental argument asks what must be true for some experience, knowledge, or practice to be possible. Kant's arguments about space, time, and categories are influential examples. A common form says: experience or judgment occurs; it requires condition C; therefore C must obtain. The difficult step is showing that C is genuinely necessary and that no alternative condition could do the work.
arguments.origin: Immanuel Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (1781/1787); forms of transcendental reasoning predate Kant.
premises: A specified experience or practice is occurring.
That experience or practice is possible only if condition C obtains.
No alternative condition could perform the necessary role attributed to C.
arguments.conclusion: Condition C obtains as a necessary condition for the specified experience or practice.
assumptions: The target experience or practice is accurately described.
The proposed condition is necessary rather than merely one familiar explanation.
The conclusion concerns conditions of possibility and may not establish a mind-independent metaphysical reality without additional premises.

objections.objection: The proposed condition may be one possible explanation rather than a necessary one.
objections.reply: A defender must show that alternatives fail; mapping the argument's conditions makes that burden visible.

objections.objection: The conclusion may concern how we must think, not how reality is independently structured.
objections.reply: A Kantian can accept a distinction between conditions of experience and things as they are in themselves; the argument's reach must be stated accordingly.

objections.objection: The argument can beg the question by building its conclusion into the description of experience.
objections.reply: A defender can argue that the condition is independently demonstrated through the practice's structure, but that demonstration needs scrutiny.

examples.text: If objective experience requires ordering events in time, one argues that temporal ordering is a condition of that experience.
examples.note: The example shows the inference pattern; whether time is a condition of experience or a feature of reality is a further issue.

arguments.name: Utility monster argument
arguments.summary: A being that gains far more utility from each resource could absorb everything under simple total-utility maximization.
arguments.body: Nozick imagines a utility monster that receives vastly more benefit from resources than everyone else. If morality requires maximizing the sum of utility, transferring resources to the monster may be required no matter how much others lose. The case challenges whether aggregate utility alone captures fairness and the separateness of persons. It is an objection to a simple maximizing principle, not a proof that every consequentialist theory endorses unequal allocation.
arguments.origin: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), chapter 3.
premises: A simple act-utilitarian principle requires choosing the outcome with the greatest total utility.
A possible recipient gains far more utility from each resource than anyone else loses by giving it up.
Repeated transfers to that recipient maximize aggregate utility.
arguments.conclusion: Simple aggregate utility maximization can recommend distributions many find unjust, so it needs defense or revision.
assumptions: Utility can be compared across persons and summed.
The imagined monster's unusually high marginal utility is coherent and relevant to moral theory.
Intuitive resistance to the result is evidence against the principle, rather than merely a preference for familiar distributions.

objections.objection: A utility monster may be impossible or empirically implausible.
objections.reply: A defender of the objection treats the case as a test of principle, while acknowledging that implausibility limits its practical force.

objections.objection: Rule consequentialism or prioritarianism can avoid the result.
objections.reply: That concedes the case challenges simple aggregate act-utilitarianism rather than consequentialism as a whole.

objections.objection: If the monster truly gains more, maximizing total utility may correctly favor it.
objections.reply: The objection asks whether maximizing totals is an adequate moral standard when it permits one person's interests to swamp everyone else's.

examples.text: One person gets ten units of benefit from each resource while each of many others loses one unit.
examples.note: A sufficiently large difference can make aggregate maximization direct nearly all resources to the one person.

arguments.name: Veil of ignorance argument
arguments.summary: Principles chosen without knowing one's social position are argued to be fairer than rules tailored to known advantage.
arguments.body: Rawls asks parties to choose principles for society behind a veil that hides their class, race, talents, religion, and conception of the good. Because no one can tailor the rules to their own known position, the choice models impartiality. Rawls argues that such parties would select equal basic liberties and permit inequalities only under conditions including fair opportunity and benefit to the least advantaged. The thought experiment is a device for testing principles, not a claim about a historical contract.
arguments.origin: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971), especially the original position and veil of ignorance.
premises: Principles of justice should not depend on morally arbitrary advantages such as birth or social class.
Parties behind the veil do not know which social position or natural talents they will have.
Rational parties seek adequate protection for their interests under uncertainty.
The chosen principles should be acceptable as fair terms of cooperation.
arguments.conclusion: The original position supports equal basic liberties and constraints on social and economic inequalities, including concern for the least advantaged.
assumptions: The information excluded by the veil is morally arbitrary for selecting principles.
The model of rational choice and uncertainty captures fairness rather than imposing a contested risk attitude.
The original position is a justificatory model, not a prediction of actual agreement.

objections.objection: Risk-averse parties may choose a maximin rule even when expected outcomes favor another principle.
objections.reply: Rawls argues that features of the choice situation make maximin appropriate; critics dispute whether the assumptions warrant that strategy.

objections.objection: The veil hides information needed to tailor useful institutions to real circumstances.
objections.reply: Rawls's parties retain general social and economic knowledge; the veil removes personal bargaining advantages, not all relevant facts.

objections.objection: The setup already encodes liberal egalitarian values and so cannot neutrally derive them.
objections.reply: A defender can present it as a reflective-equilibrium test of principles, not a value-free deduction from nothing.

examples.text: A policymaker must choose rules without knowing whether they will be rich or poor, healthy or disabled.
examples.note: The information restriction tests whether the rules can be justified without knowing one's place under them.
